---SIGNAL 1---
NAME: Solvency-Screened Book-to-Market
EXPRESSION: SUMRANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), SUMRANK(RATIO(re, at), RATIO(che, ADD(dltt, dlc))))
HYPOTHESIS: Cheapness earns a premium only when the balance sheet shows accumulated profitability (retained earnings) and liquid resources able to service debt; jointly ranking cheapness with these two solvency channels isolates compensated value from distressed value traps.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
REASONING: Book-to-market alone mixes healthy cheap firms with firms priced for default, so the ranked union with retained-earnings capitalization and cash-to-debt coverage tilts the long leg toward solvent cheap firms and the short leg toward expensive levered firms. Ranking each channel makes the composite robust to the fat tails of che/debt and BM. The interaction is genuine because a firm scores high only if it is simultaneously cheap and financially resilient.
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite

---SIGNAL 2---
NAME: Value Gated by Going-Concern Flags
EXPRESSION: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1), ADD(INDICATOR(re, 0), INDICATOR(SUB(act, lct), 0)))
HYPOTHESIS: The value premium is conditional: it accrues to cheap firms with positive retained earnings and positive working capital, while cheap firms failing both going-concern screens have valuations that reflect genuine default risk and earn no premium.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
REASONING: The indicator sum acts as a 0/1/2 multiplier that switches the value exposure off for firms with a deficit in accumulated earnings and a liquidity shortfall, so extreme cheapness among distressed firms is collapsed to the bottom of the cross-section. This is an explicitly conditional interaction rather than an additive blend of two effects. Winsorizing book-to-market prevents a handful of near-zero-market-cap firms from dominating the long leg.
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional

---SIGNAL 3---
NAME: EBITDA to Net-Debt-Adjusted Enterprise Value
EXPRESSION: RATIO(ebitda, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))
HYPOTHESIS: Cheapness should be measured against the claims of all capital providers; a firm that looks cheap on equity price but carries large net debt is not cheap, it is levered, and the mispricing correction accrues to firms cheap on an enterprise basis.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
REASONING: Embedding debt minus cash directly in the valuation denominator makes the distress dimension change the price metric itself rather than serving as a separate screen, so equity-cheap but net-debt-heavy firms are demoted while cash-rich cheap firms are promoted. This mechanically separates operating-cash-flow value from leverage-induced optical value. EBITDA is used as the numerator because it is the claim-neutral cash flow available to all capital.
INTERACTION_TYPE: ratio

---SIGNAL 4---
NAME: Cheapness Times Net Cash Buffer
EXPRESSION: MUL(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), at)))
HYPOTHESIS: The return to cheapness is increasing in the firm's net cash position: the same book-to-market signals mispricing when the firm holds net cash and signals impending equity dilution or default when the firm holds net debt.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
REASONING: A product of two industry-demeaned z-scores is a pure interaction term whose sign flips with the sign of the net-cash buffer, so cheap net-debtors are shorted alongside expensive net-cash firms. Industry standardization removes the mechanical correlation between sector leverage norms and sector valuation multiples. This tests whether the value effect is genuinely state-dependent rather than merely additive with a leverage control.
INTERACTION_TYPE: novel

---SIGNAL 5---
NAME: Cheapness Times Deleveraging
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(lt, at), 1), 1)))
HYPOTHESIS: What separates value opportunities from traps is the direction of the distress state: cheap firms actively reducing their liability burden are recovering and repricing upward, while equally cheap firms whose leverage is rising are sliding toward distress.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
REASONING: The cheapness rank sets the magnitude of the bet and the year-over-year change in the liabilities-to-assets ratio sets its direction, so the signal goes long cheap deleveraging firms and short cheap re-levering firms. This uses a change-in-distress state rather than a level screen, capturing information that static leverage filters miss. Winsorizing the leverage change limits distortion from restructurings and large acquisitions.
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional

---SIGNAL 6---
NAME: Cheap Chronic Loss Trap
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(NEG(ib), 0), 5))
HYPOTHESIS: Deep cheapness accompanied by repeated annual losses identifies lottery-like distressed equities whose low price reflects a persistent inability to generate earnings; these firms underperform despite apparently attractive multiples.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: Counting loss years over five fiscal years measures the persistence, not just the presence, of financial trouble, and multiplying by the cheapness rank isolates the specific cell of the value/distress grid where the trap story applies. Profitable cheap firms score zero and are separated from chronically unprofitable cheap firms that score high, so the signal is short-side driven and predicts low returns.
INTERACTION_TYPE: novel

---CRITIQUE Solvency-Screened Book-to-Market---
VERDICT: flag
SCORE: 2
RATIONALE: SUMRANK is an additive, fully compensatory blend, so the stated claim that "a firm scores high only if it is simultaneously cheap and financially resilient" is false — a very cheap firm with terrible solvency still ranks high — and the construct is in any case a well-trodden value-plus-quality (retained-earnings / cash-coverage) composite.

---CRITIQUE Value Gated by Going-Concern Flags---
VERDICT: accept
SCORE: 3
RATIONALE: The 0/1/2 multiplier is a genuinely conditional switch and the expression matches the hypothesis, but it is close in spirit to Piotroski-style value screening and the short leg becomes an undifferentiated mass of zero-flag firms regardless of valuation, so the alpha may be driven by a plain distress short rather than by conditioning the value premium.

---CRITIQUE EBITDA to Net-Debt-Adjusted Enterprise Value---
VERDICT: flag
SCORE: 2
RATIONALE: This is EBITDA/EV, a directly published and heavily replicated value anomaly (Loughran–Wellman, Gray–Vogel), not a cross-theme discovery, and the unguarded denominator can approach zero or turn negative for highly cash-rich firms, producing sign-flipped extremes.

---CRITIQUE Cheapness Times Net Cash Buffer---
VERDICT: flag
SCORE: 3
RATIONALE: A bare product of two z-scores is sign-symmetric, so the long leg pools cheap net-cash firms with *expensive net-debt* firms — exactly the quadrant the hypothesis calls most distressed — which the reasoning silently omits and which contradicts the expected sign.

---CRITIQUE Cheapness Times Deleveraging---
VERDICT: accept
SCORE: 3
RATIONALE: The magnitude-times-direction construction is internally consistent and change-in-leverage conditioning on value is a defensible cross-theme test, though it overlaps the known net-debt-issuance/financing anomaly and its behavior hinges on whether RANK is nonnegative or centered (a centered rank would flip the sign for expensive firms and break the stated logic).

---CRITIQUE Cheap Chronic Loss Trap---
VERDICT: accept
SCORE: 3
RATIONALE: The loss-persistence-times-cheapness cell is a coherent value-trap test with a correctly signed expression, but roughly two-thirds of firms will score exactly zero, so the "long" leg is a large tie block and the resulting spread is essentially a short-only distress bet that may add little beyond the known financial-distress anomaly.

---SIGNAL 1---
NAME: Weakest-Link Value Solvency Score
EXPRESSION: MIN(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(re, at), RATIO(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)))))
HYPOTHESIS: Compensated value requires cheapness and solvency jointly, so the firm's score should be its worst dimension: a deeply cheap firm with no accumulated earnings and no cash relative to debt is a distress trap, not a value opportunity, and must not be rescued by its cheapness rank.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional
REASONING: Replacing the additive SUMRANK blend with MIN of the two ranked dimensions makes the score non-compensatory, so a firm ranks high only if it is simultaneously in the cheap tail and the solvent tail — the claim the earlier version could not support. Both arguments are rescaled to a common [0,1] rank metric before the MIN so neither dimension mechanically dominates the binding constraint. The short leg is now firms that are weak on at least one dimension, which is precisely the expensive-or-distressed population the economic story targets.

---SIGNAL 2---
NAME: Cash Yield Net of Near-Term Debt Maturities
EXPRESSION: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dlc), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)
HYPOTHESIS: What shareholders actually own is operating cash flow left over after creditors' imminent claims are met; a cheap price attached to cash flow that is fully absorbed by debt coming due within the year is a refinancing-risk trap rather than a value opportunity.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
INTERACTION_TYPE: ratio
REASONING: This is not the published EBITDA/EV multiple: the distress variable enters the numerator as a claim that consumes cash flow (debt in current liabilities), so the metric measures residual cash yield to equity after near-term debt service rather than restating the capitalization denominator. The denominator is market capitalization, which is strictly positive, eliminating the sign-flip and near-zero-denominator pathology of an enterprise-value deflator. Winsorizing at the 1% tails controls micro-cap yield explosions while preserving full coverage of firms reporting cash flow statements.

---SIGNAL 3---
NAME: Net-Leverage-Adjusted Residual Cheapness
EXPRESSION: SUB(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dltt, dlc), che), at)))
HYPOTHESIS: Net debt rationally justifies part of a firm's cheapness, so only the cheapness that exceeds what its net leverage warrants is mispricing; firms cheap despite carrying little net debt are the compensated value cases, firms expensive despite heavy net debt are the overpriced distressed cases.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
INTERACTION_TYPE: novel
REASONING: The earlier z-score product was sign-symmetric and polluted the long leg with expensive net-debt firms; differencing ranks instead makes the signal monotonically increasing in cheapness and monotonically decreasing in net leverage, so the long leg is unambiguously cheap-and-unlevered and the short leg is expensive-and-net-indebted. Netting cash against total debt before scaling by assets captures true default exposure rather than gross borrowing, distinguishing cash-rich borrowers from genuinely strained ones. Rank transformation of both legs keeps the difference well scaled and immune to the fat tails in leverage and book-to-market.
